attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post. He restates his 2022 argument and asserts its current status himself.

semantics.note: The 'still hasn't' aside is a present-status observation that scaling pretraining data and compute alone has not solved reasoning, misalignment and hallucinations. The normalised claim keeps the 'alone' qualifier and all three problem areas.

contract.note: Requiring evidence that isolates pretraining is a defensible reading of 'alone', but it is strict. Whether failures of post-trained models count largely decides the result. 'Solved' has no threshold.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own GPT-4.5 announcement (Feb 2025). It reports reasoning gains from scaling and leaves errors in place (36.7% AIME). The model was also changed in post-training, so it is not a clean test of pretraining alone.

GPT-4.5 system card, a company disclosure. It reports a 19% PersonQA hallucination rate and weak StrongReject scores. The model was trained with SFT and RLHF, so the results do not isolate pretraining scale.

reviews.rationale: Both items are OpenAI disclosures about a model trained with more than pretraining. They show remaining reasoning errors, hallucinations and jailbreak weaknesses, but the contract requires evaluations that isolate pretraining-only scaling, and the packet has none. Nothing shows a pretraining-only system reliably solving these problems either. The packet does not settle the claim on the contract's terms.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post. 'Them' refers to LLMs.

semantics.note: A firm but sweeping claim about how funding is allocated. The normalised claim keeps 'nearly all' and 'making them larger'. It is close to hyperbole but is stated as fact.

contract.note: The plain reading (an overwhelming share of AI funding going solely to scaling LLMs, calendar 2024) is ordinary. But the speaker gave no denominator or period, and the contract's own flags show the result depends on which funding pool is used. That conflicts with its interpretation_determines_result=false.

evidence.note: Epoch AI's estimate (published Mar 2026, before the evaluation date) covers one company, OpenAI, in 2024: about 10% of R&D compute went to final training runs. Other compute may also have served scaling. It is not a measure of total AI funding.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no comprehensive record of how AI funding was allocated by purpose. The only item covers compute use at a single company and cannot measure the sector-wide share spent on making LLMs larger. The evidence neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus states this in his own voice. He cites Fei-Fei Li in support of the spatial-reasoning part but asserts both parts himself.

semantics.note: Two present-status observations, both kept: reasoning remains unreliable, and spatial reasoning is far from solved. Dropping the Fei-Fei Li citation does not change what Marcus committed to.

contract.note: The plain reading for mid-2025 (substantial documented reasoning failures, poor spatial-benchmark results) is ordinary and fair. The contradiction condition sets an appropriately high bar.

evidence.note: MindCube preprint, v1 dated 26 Jun 2025. Existing vision-language models scored near random on a large spatial-reasoning benchmark.
Apple preprint, June 2025: reasoning models' accuracy collapsed beyond certain levels of puzzle complexity. The abstract finding dates from v1.
A June 2025 rebuttal argues that the Apple failures partly reflect test design. This weakens e2 only. It does not show that reasoning was reliable and does not touch the spatial findings.

reviews.rationale: Mid-2025 preprints show near-random results on spatial reasoning (e1) and reasoning collapse on harder puzzles (e2). The rebuttal (e3) narrows the force of e2 but does not show reliable reasoning, and nothing shows spatial reasoning largely solved. Both parts of the claim hold on the plain reading.

attribution.note: This is the closing thesis of Marcus's own post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The normalised claim keeps 'accidentally' and 'without any public acknowledgement'. 'Vindicated' is an evaluative judgment, and 'accidentally' concerns intent, so only parts of the claim can be checked against evidence.

contract.note: Reading 'vindicated' as a practical benefit from symbolic tools follows Marcus's own context and is fair. The result turns on what 'acknowledgement' means and on intent, which the speaker did not define.

evidence.note: OpenAI's o3 announcement (Apr 2025, company disclosure). It reports that tool use, including Python, improves capability. This supports the practical-benefit part, but it also shows OpenAI publicly discussing the benefits of tools.
OpenAI's 2023 plugins post disclosed that ChatGPT ran a Python interpreter. It shows the tool integration was public but says nothing about whether OpenAI framed it as support for neurosymbolic AI.

reviews.rationale: The practical-benefit part is supported by OpenAI's own disclosure. The absence of 'any public acknowledgement whatsoever' was not checked against a comprehensive record, and the contract says a keyword search cannot establish it. Whether the vindication was 'accidental' cannot be tested with this evidence. The packet does not settle the claim as a whole.
